reasoning.Student A:
In most school-choice mechanisms based on submitted rankings and priorities (e.g., Deferred Acceptance / Gale-Shapley style), truth-telling is a dominant strategy — misreporting preferences cannot improve and can only hurt your assigned outcome. 

Looking at my priorities: I have top priority (rank 1) at both w and y, and lower priority (rank 2) at x and z. Since y is my most preferred school and I hold the highest priority there, ranking it first maximizes my chances of getting my top choice — even though many other applicants also favor y first, my priority advantage there works in my favor.

For the remaining schools, since DA-type mechanisms reward truthful preference revelation (any deviation could cause me to end up unmatched or in a worse school without benefit), I will submit my true preference order: y > x > w > z. This aligns my highest-preference school with my highest-priority school, giving me the best strategic position, and follows correctly with my secondary priorities at x and z.

My true preference is z > y > x > w.

Given DA's strategy-proofness, I should just submit my true preferences to maximize my chances of getting my best possible outcome.
